topic.name: Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=5$ and $\sigma_2=4.$ Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

  • First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{4}{5} \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \[ \mathbf u_3 = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\x_3 \end{bmatrix} \] such that \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_3 = 0 \\ \mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u}_3 = 0, \end{cases} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_3\|=1. \]

Solving this system, which is equivalent to \[ \begin{cases} -\dfrac{4}{5} x_2 - \dfrac{3}{5} x_3 = 0 \\ x_1 = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 4 x_2 +3x_3 = 0\\ x_1 = 0, \end{cases} \] we get the nonzero normalized solution

\[ \mathbf{u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} \\ \dfrac{4}{5} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the matrix $U \mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{ 0} \\ -\dfrac{4}{5} & 0& \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{ -\dfrac{3}{5}} \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} &0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{ \dfrac{4}{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=2\sqrt 6$ and $\sigma_2=2.$ Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

  • First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt 6} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt 6} \begin{bmatrix} 2{\sqrt{2}} \\ 2\sqrt 2 \\ 2\sqrt 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 3} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt 2 \\ 0 \\ -{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \[ \mathbf u_3 = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\x_3 \end{bmatrix} \] such that \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_3 = 0 \\ \mathbf{u}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u}_3 = 0, \end{cases} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_3\|=1. \]

Solving this system, which is equivalent to \[ \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} x_1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} x_2 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} x_3 = 0 \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0 \\ x_1 - x_3 = 0, \end{cases} \] we get the nonzero normalized solution

\[ \mathbf{u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 6} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt 6} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 6} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we construct the matrix $U \mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 3} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt 6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt 6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt 6}} \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 3\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=3\sqrt{2}$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{2}{3}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{2}{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{3} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

\[ \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix} \]

such that $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1.$

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ \dfrac{2}{3} x_1 - \dfrac{2}{3} x_2 + \dfrac{1}{3} x_3 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{2x_1 - 2x_2 + x_3 = 0}, \] we get the general solution

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_1} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_2} \\ -2x_1+2x_2 \end{bmatrix} = x_1 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_1} + x_2 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_2}, \]

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ are not mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we have to orthogonalize them using the Gram-Schmidt process. So, let \[ \mathbf{c}_1=\mathbf{b}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Then, \begin{align*} \mathbf{c}_2 &= \mathbf{b}_2 - \dfrac{\mathbf{b}_2 \cdot \mathbf{c}_1}{\mathbf{c}_1 \cdot \mathbf{c}_1}\mathbf{c}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{(-4)}5 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{4} \\ 5 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{2} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Finally, normalizing orthogonal vectors $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain the second and third columns of $U{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}} \\ 0 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt{5}}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{5}{3\sqrt{5}}} \\ \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following: \[ U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{4}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{3} & 0 & \dfrac{5}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{3} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{5}} \\ \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ select the correct options in the computations of the matrix $U$ below.
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

  • $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

  • $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

  • $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=2$ and $\sigma_2=0.$ Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors

\[ \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3\end{bmatrix} \]

such that $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1.$

Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} x_2 = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_1 - x_2 = 0}, \] we get the general solution

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_2} \\ x_2 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{x_3} \end{bmatrix} = x_2 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_1} + x_3 \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\large \mathbf{b}_2}, \]

where $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U{:}$

\[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \end{bmatrix} \qquad \mathbf{u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} \\ 0 \\ \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{1} \end{bmatrix} \]

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following: \[ U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
